item.title: Paris game played in festive atmosphere after fresh demonstrations
item.description: Protests largely overshadowed the build-up to the first NFL regular-season game.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Daheron
item.content:encoded: The Pittsburgh Steelers defeated the New Orleans Saints 16-10 in the first NFL regular-season game in Paris on Sunday, in a calm and festive atmosphere, a day after fresh demonstrations drew more than 100,000 people into the French capital. The nationwide protests largely overshadowed the build-up to the game, with some fan and NFL [USN:L6N46912R TEXT:"events cancelled"] over the weekend, mainly due to their location in central Paris. On Sunday, as Saturday’s rain gave way to sunshine, the mood was peaceful before kickoff around the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, some 10km (6 miles) north of Paris centre and more than 13km (8 miles) from Porte d'Italie, where Saturday's protests began in southern Paris. James Brown, a 51-year-old Saints fan who travelled to Paris especially for the game, told Reuters the atmosphere around the stadium was "wonderful, really good". The police presence appeared neither heavy nor unusual at the Stade de France, which hosted rugby sevens and athletics during the 2024 Paris Olympics and regularly serves as the home ground for the French national rugby and soccer teams. Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week's unrest. The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality. "We didn't notice much yesterday," 38-year-old Steelers fan Lukas Baldridge told Reuters. "We came in, went to a bar, got some drinks, got dinner, went home, didn't see any protesting. "Streets were closed. Most shops were closed. That felt unusual maybe but I don't know enough about Paris to know what is normal and what's not normal." The party was in full swing in a packed stadium when the game kicked off at 2.30 p.m. (1330 GMT), after French stars Antoine Dupont and Teddy Riner were introduced to the crowd. A couple of hours earlier, some Steelers players had arrived at the Stade de France dressed like characters from Peaky Blinders. Steelers fans seemed to outnumber their opponents, even though the neutral-site game was officially hosted by the Saints. "It kind of felt 50/50," Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss told a press conference. "This is such a fun atmosphere. Maybe not feel like the true home team, it was a very special atmosphere, one I wish we could have gotten a win in." Nigerian rapper Burna Boy and French singer Yseult performed during a brief halftime show. "I would like to start by saying how much we appreciate everyone who, in the country of France, Paris, Versailles, helped make this event happen," Saints coach Kellen Moore told a press conference. "I thought it was a really great event, really great game today."

item.title: What are Brazilian voters' main concerns?
item.description: Brazilians headed to the ballot box on Sunday, in a runoff vote that pits right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
item.dc:creator: Isabel Teles
item.content:encoded: Brazilians headed to the ballot box on Sunday, in a runoff vote that pits right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Here are the main themes that have driven the campaign: INFLATION Cost-of-living concerns are widespread. More than two-thirds of respondents told a Quaest poll in August their purchasing power [USN:L6N459162 TEXT:"had declined"] versus the previous year. Annual inflation stood at 4.58% in the 12 months through September, above the central bank's 3% target, pushing prices — including for food — higher Lula has pledged to implement measures to allow for steady cuts in borrowing costs and keep inflation under control Bolsonaro wants to reduce and stabilize public debt to bring interest rates closer to international levels and steer inflation toward the central bank's target CRIME Crime is another major [USN:L1N45Z0NR TEXT:"concern"] for Brazilians. While Brazil's homicide rate fell by 40% over the last decade, improvements in fighting crime have been uneven, according to the Brazilian Public Security Forum, a think tank. Bolsonaro has pledged a heavy-handed approach to criminals, promising maximum-security prisons and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses Lula wants to increase the federal prison system's capacity to hold gang leaders, while still investing in poor areas to reduce the influence of organized crime CORRUPTION Corruption is also at the top of voters' minds, with both Lula's circle and Bolsonaro [USN:L6N46611M TEXT:"facing scrutiny"] in high-profile cases. A major scandal that led to the collapse of mid-size lender Banco Master has sparked multiple probes, including into [USN:L6N3ZZ1EP TEXT:"Bolsonaro"] over alleged corruption and money laundering, accusations he denies Bolsonaro has pledged to fight corruption by shielding state-run companies and pension funds from political appointments and expanding transparency in public spending Lula has vowed to deepen anti-corruption and transparency policies even as his son - who has denied the allegations - is being investigated in probes involving alleged influence peddling, corruption and fraud PUBLIC FINANCES Brazil's public finances are under pressure, especially due to pensions and social benefits. The difficult fiscal outlook has sparked fears of welfare cuts, while many Brazilians are struggling with debt arrears due to years of double-digit interest rates. Public debt has risen by more than 10 percentage points during Lula's current term, reaching [USN:L1N45M0ES TEXT:"82.9%"] of gross domestic product Brazil's benchmark interest rate of [USN:L6N458186 TEXT:"13.75%"] remains among the highest in the world Long-term interest rates [USN:L1N45R06Y TEXT:"fell sharply"] after Bolsonaro's stronger-than-expected first-round performance He has promised to ramp up [USN:L1N4580UE TEXT:"fiscal adjustment"], targeting 1.5% of GDP improvement in the primary balance within 18 months to lower borrowing costs Lula has reiterated commitments to improve Brazil's primary balance targeting an [USN:L1N44S10B TEXT:"effective surplus"] near 1.3% of GDP by 2030, versus a projected 0.4% deficit this year FOREIGN POLICY After US President Donald Trump imposed [USN:L6N3TR0ZD TEXT:"tariffs"] on a swathe of Brazilian goods in 2025, foreign policy became a more prominent issue for many Brazilians. Bolsonaro has courted Trump and other right-wing allies globally He wants to rebuild ties with Argentina, the US and Israel, arguing relations with each are close to breaking point Lula has campaigned for a foreign policy based on multilateralism and stronger ties with the Mercosur bloc of South American states and the BRICS nations ($1 = 5.0086 reais)

item.title: French protest groups demand more rallies as Macron faces tough choices
item.description: The government began talks with unions and student representatives to defuse the crisis, but protest leaders say the measures it has proposed are inadequate.
item.dc:creator: Crispian Balmer, Juliette Jabkhiro
item.content:encoded: French protest groups and unions called on Sunday for further demonstrations as they sought to maintain pressure on the government after a huge security operation helped to contain unrest during nationwide rallies on Saturday. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in Saturday's marches as authorities deployed 70,000 police, helping to avert a repeat of the looting and vandalism that swept many cities on October 17. Labour leaders urged further protests next Saturday and a nationwide strike on November 5, saying frustration over wages, living costs and public services was spreading far beyond the student movement that first mobilised last month. "We see an aggregation of anger," Murielle Guilbert, co-leader of the left-wing Solidaires trade union federation, told BFM TV. She said grievances from students, workers, firefighters and other groups were converging. "We call on people to take to the streets next Saturday." The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstration while the large CGT union said it would decide during the week. MACRON'S SCOPE TO RESPOND IS MINIMAL The Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes, also called for mass rallies next Saturday, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly. "There is anger in this country. It's growing in schools and universities, on roundabouts, in neighbourhoods, on farms and in workplaces," activist Azelma Sigaux told reporters. In 2019, President Emmanuel Macron was able to find the resources to reduce fuel costs in response to the Yellow Vests. Seven years on, strained public finances leave him with little room to meet protesters' demands. His mandate also expires next April and his centrist party no longer has the majority needed to pass major legislation. The government has begun talks with unions and student representatives to try to defuse the crisis, but protest leaders say the measures it has proposed so far are inadequate. "We have received no response at all from this government," said Guilbert. Police unions said on Sunday they did not have enough staff to maintain for any length of time the high level of deployment that on Saturday helped to limit disorder to sporadic clashes in a number of cities, including Paris and Marseille. Some 1,314 people were arrested on Saturday, half of last week's numbers, the interior ministry said on Sunday, and about 50 police were injured, compared with more than 1,000 last week. The protests have resonated beyond France's borders. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators. [USN:FWN4630JL TEXT:"In Albania"], peaceful protests that began at the end of May this month turned into violent unrest and skirmishes have taken place in several Italian cities for a second week running.

item.title: Brasil acude a las urnas en reñido balotaje presidencial entre Lula y Flávio Bolsonaro
item.description: Los brasileños votaban el domingo en una reñida segunda vuelta electoral que podría inclinar bruscamente a la derecha a la nación más grande de América Latina, acercándola a Estados Unidos como parte de un giro conservador más amplio en toda la región.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin
item.content:encoded: Los brasileños votaban el domingo en una reñida segunda vuelta electoral que podría inclinar bruscamente a la derecha a la nación más grande de América Latina, acercándola a Estados Unidos como parte de un giro conservador más amplio en toda la región. El balotaje enfrenta al presidente izquierdista Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva con el senador derechista Flávio Bolsonaro. El hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro dio la sorpresa a principios de mes al liderar la votación en la primera vuelta en contra de lo que decían las encuestas. La tensión era alta, ya que las encuestas pronosticaban una contienda increíblemente reñida, y ambos candidatos solicitaron a última hora a las autoridades electorales que ampliaran el horario de votación en dos horas en determinados estados. Bolsonaro solicitó tiempo adicional en tres estados, alegando mal clima, mientras que Lula pidió que ampliaran el horario de votación en nueve estados después de que su campaña denunciara que las autoridades habían reducido el servicio de transporte público el día de las elecciones. Muchos brasileños dependen del transporte público para votar en las ciudades en las que están empadronados, pero en las que quizá no residan. Los seguidores de Lula suelen depender en mayor medida del transporte público en estas ciudades. Un tribunal del estado de Bahía, bastión de Lula en el noreste, ordenó la detención de un alto cargo del transporte en Salvador por las acusaciones de que ordenó una reducción de la flota de autobuses de la ciudad. "Nadie debería renunciar a votar porque algún empresario sin escrúpulos o algún alcalde corrupto y deshonesto haya intentado impedírselo", declaró Lula a periodistas. Un triunfo de Bolsonaro, de 45 años, prolongaría la ola de victorias de la derecha para los candidatos latinoamericanos afines a Donald Trump, mientras que un cuarto mandato para Lula sería una decepción en Washington, que ha tenido roces con su gobierno en materia de comercio y seguridad. Reuters reveló el sábado una campaña dentro del Departamento de Estado de Trump para ayudar a que los Bolsonaro volvieran al poder. La contienda electoral ha estado marcada por escándalos de corrupción, incertidumbre económica y acusaciones de injerencia estadounidense, algo que Washington niega. También se ha visto influenciada por las repercusiones de la condena de Jair Bolsonaro en 2025 por planear un golpe de Estado en 2022, ante la promesa de Flávio de liberar a su padre si resulta elegido. Trump calificó el caso de "caza de brujas" e impuso un arancel del 50% a Brasil en 2025, en una decisión vinculada explícitamente al juicio de Jair Bolsonaro. Si bien muchas de estas medidas fueron posteriormente suavizadas, el mandatario republicano impuso nuevos aranceles a Brasil este año, alegando prácticas comerciales desleales. Lula ha presentado la cercanía del Gobierno de Trump con el clan Bolsonaro como parte de un intento de influir en las elecciones, al tiempo que ha calificado los aranceles y otras medidas punitivas de intimidación. "No podemos entregar Brasil", afirmó Elenildes dos Reis, una abogada de 60 años de São Paulo que votó por Lula y señaló que su victoria sería una forma de plantarle cara a Trump y a lo que ella describió como una ola creciente de fascismo. "No será solo nuestra victoria, será la del mundo", añadió. En materia económica, a pesar de la disminución de la desigualdad y el desempleo, Lula ha tenido dificultades para ganarse a un electorado que lidia con el alto costo de la vida y las elevadas deudas familiares. La violencia endémica de las pandillas también preocupa a los votantes. RESULTADO INCIERTO Bolsonaro ha intentado sacar provecho de la preocupación por el costo de la vida y también ha prometido mano dura para combatir la delincuencia, comprometiéndose a construir cárceles de máxima seguridad y a aplicar la castración química para los delitos sexuales graves. "Necesitamos un cambio", afirmó José Carlos Jarra, un jubilado de 61 años de São Paulo que trabajó en el sector sanitario y votó a Bolsonaro. Dijo esperar que el senador abordara la seguridad pública y hiciera más por los jubilados, y calificó el salario mínimo de Brasil como "una vergüenza". En Río de Janeiro, Alba Marques, una jubilada de 75 años, afirmó que su voto por Bolsonaro era un voto en contra del Partido de los Trabajadores de Lula, no a favor del senador. "Ya no soporto que, desde hace 40 años, un tipo diga que va a arreglar Brasil. Siempre la misma promesa", afirmó. Al emitir su voto en Río de Janeiro el domingo, Flávio Bolsonaro instó a la gente a acudir a las urnas "con lluvia o con sol". Lula, por su parte, votará en São Bernardo do Campo, cerca de São Paulo. Las encuestas muestran que los candidatos están prácticamente empatados de cara a la segunda vuelta, con recortando distancias en los últimos días. Lula votó en São Bernardo do Campo, cerca de São Paulo, y agradeció a sus seguidores. "Lo que la gente ha hecho por mí estos últimos días es algo que nunca podré devolver", dijo a periodistas. Los precedentes históricos favorecen a Bolsonaro, ya que ningún candidato ha ganado la presidencia tras quedar segundo en la primera vuelta de las elecciones. Bolsonaro obtuvo el 47% de los votos emitidos en la primera vuelta, contra e 45% de Lula. La victoria del senador disparó los mercados brasileños y su moneda ante las expectativas de reformas favorables a las empresas. Su éxito en la primera vuelta se vio reflejado en las elecciones al Congreso de su Partido Liberal y de otros políticos de derecha, lo que podría allanarle el camino legislativo o complicarle la gobernabilidad a Lula.

item.title: Rybakina brushes aside Fernandez to retain Ningbo crown
item.description: The title is her first as world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Elena Rybakina blazed past unseeded Canadian Leylah Fernandez 6-2 6-2 in the Ningbo Open final on Sunday to retain her title and lift her first trophy as the world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month. The victory in Ningbo also helped the Kazakh to take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking, further burnishing a spectacular season in which she won the Australian Open title before adding the US Open crown to reach the summit. "It's amazing to play in front of you... it's my second year here and my second win," Rybakina told the crowd in the eastern Chinese city after collecting a tour-leading fourth title of the season and 15th overall. "It's such a special place for me. Thanks so much Ningbo." Rybakina's latest triumph is a timely lift after setbacks in Beijing and Wuhan, as she turns her attention to the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo this week before she launches her title defence at the season finale in Indian Wells, California, from November 8. TRADEMARK POWER Top seed Rybakina made the breakthrough with her trademark power in the fifth game and then unleashed a searing crosscourt backhand winner to go 4-2 up, before the 27-year-old wrapped up the opening set in 38 minutes. World number 30 Fernandez made a bright start to the next set but Rybakina absorbed the pressure and raised her level to force an error and break for 2-1, with the three-times Grand Slam champion breezing to victory from there. Fernandez, who won the Singapore Open last month, remained upbeat despite a disappointing showing in the final and backed herself to finish the season strongly after a gruelling run of matches in Ningbo. "I'd like to congratulate Elena for a wonderful week and a wonderful year. Congratulations to you and your team," the 24-year-old said, before addressing her own team. "We're having a good end of year. We've just got to keep going and keep working hard."

item.title: Disputa acirrada entre Flávio e Lula pode ser definida pela abstenção; cidades enfrentam problemas no transporte
item.description: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) decidem neste domingo quem governará o Brasil a partir de 5 de janeiro de 2027 após uma das campanhas eleitorais mais tensas e recheadas de acusações da história da política brasileira, sem que as pesquisas apontem um favorito claro e com um provável papel decisivo do comparecimento dos eleitores às urnas.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) decidem neste domingo quem governará o Brasil a partir de 5 de janeiro de 2027 após uma das campanhas eleitorais mais tensas e recheadas de acusações da história da política brasileira, sem que as pesquisas apontem um favorito claro e com um provável papel decisivo do comparecimento dos eleitores às urnas. Neste cenário, algumas cidades do país enfrentavam problemas no transporte público, e a Justiça eleitoral determinou a [USN:L2N46B04J TEXT:"prisão"] de um secretário municipal de Salvador sob acusação de restrição de transporte público. Flávio Bolsonaro, senador de 45 anos e filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, largou na frente na disputa pelo Planalto após um resultado surpreendente no primeiro turno, disputado há três semanas, quando terminou na liderança com 47,03% dos votos, contra 45,16% de Lula. O atual presidente e candidato à reeleição, que completará 81 anos na próxima terça-feira e que busca um quarto mandato presidencial, reduziu gradativamente a distância para o rival nas pesquisas de intenção de voto mais recentes, o que leva a corrida a um cenário incerto. “O que o povo fez comigo nesses dias é uma coisa que não tem como pagar, é muita generosidade, é muito carinho, é muito amor e eu serei eternamente grato ao comportamento do povo”, disse o petista a jornalistas após votar na manhã deste domingo, em São Bernardo do Campo (SP), berço político do Partido dos Trabalhadores. As [USN:L2N46A047 TEXT:"pesquisas divulgadas na véspera"] da votação deste domingo mostraram um empate técnico com vantagem numérica de Flávio sobre Lula de no máximo dois pontos percentuais nos votos válidos, com 51% a 49%. "Flávio é ligeiramente favorito, ele não é francamente favorito", disse o cientista político Carlos Melo, do Insper. "Quando você olha para as pesquisas, mais do que o número você tem que olhar para a tendência. A tendência é o Flávio caindo, ou praticamente paralisado, e o Lula subindo muito devagar", acrescentou, apontando que não é possível prever se essa tendência resultará em uma virada a favor de Lula neste domingo. Um dos fatores cruciais a ser observado, na avaliação de Melo, será o comparecimento às urnas, já que historicamente o eleitorado que tende a apoiar mais Lula e o PT costuma ter um comparecimento menor. Não à toa, a campanha de Lula vem concentrando esforços em incentivar pessoas que não votaram no primeiro turno a comparecerem na seção eleitoral neste domingo. No primeiro turno, mais de 33,4 milhões de eleitores não foram votar, uma abstenção de 21,08%, em um total de mais de 158,7 milhões de eleitores aptos a votar. Neste domingo, Flávio Bolsonaro também fez um apelo para que os eleitores compareçam às urnas. "Faça chuva ou faça sol, bora sair de casa para votar, que o Brasil vai mudar e o Brasil vai vencer", disse o senador, após votar no Rio de Janeiro, repetindo apelo já feito em suas redes sociais na véspera, em meio à previsão de chuvas fortes nas regiões Sul e Sudeste, onde teve desempenho melhor que Lula. "Chegou a hora da mudança de verdade", afirmou o candidato, ao lado da esposa Fernanda e da mãe, Rogéria. ÔNIBUS Em uma campanha marcada por grande movimentação das duas campanhas contra os adversários no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), que levou o presidente da corte Kassio Nunes Marques a pedir que as campanhas moderassem a quantidade de ações, há receios de que, independentemente do vencedor, ocorram novos embates mesmo após a declaração do resultado. A expectativa de uma margem apertada a favor do eleito também leva a crer que isso possa ocorrer. "A expectativa é de que vai ser uma eleição tensa", disse Creomar de Souza, analista político da Dharma Political Risk. "Acho que a gente ainda vai ter algum nível de discussão política, algum nível de embate jurídico", avaliou. Em meio a essas expectativas, Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais tiveram que agir para sanar problemas no transporte público. O presidente do TRE da Bahia, Mauricio Szporer, [USN:L2N46B04J TEXT:"determinou"] no início da tarde deste domingo a prisão do secretário municipal de Mobilidade de Salvador (Semob), Pablo Souza, sob acusação de ter orientado a redução da frota de ônibus na cidade no dia do segundo turno das eleições. Lula teve mais de 65% dos votos válidos no primeiro turno em Salvador, cujo prefeito, Bruno Reis, é do União Brasil. Em São Paulo, o TRE atendeu a um pedido do PSOL e determinou que a prefeitura colocasse 100% da frota de ônibus para circular neste domingo, com multa de R$100 mil ao prefeito e ao presidente da SPTrans em caso de descumprimento. Em declaração a jornalistas, Lula disse que não aceitaria essa situação. "Não vamos aceitar banditismo e mau-caratismo nem de prefeito, nem de governador", disse o presidente. Ele aproveitou para fazer um apelo que os eleitores não deixem de votar: "Não desistam de votar, esperem e votem". Em entrevista à imprensa, Nunes Marques afirmou que há demanda no TSE para prolongar o período de votação do segundo turno e, sem dar detalhes, disse que "isso certamente, como toda e qualquer ação, será analisado a seu tempo". "De fato, em alguns locais há uma dificuldade ainda no transporte, já está sendo corrigida", disse. Ele acrescentou que o TSE está recebendo, periodicamente, relatórios do TRE da Bahia. DEMOCRACIA E MUDANÇA Eleitores relatavam uma votação sem as filas vistas no primeiro turno, quando foi preciso votar também para deputado federal e estadual, senadores e governador. Neste segundo turno, apenas cinco Estados e o Distrito Federal têm votação para governador, além da eleição para presidente. A bibliotecária aposentada Hilda Corrêa, de 80 anos, fez questão de votar em Brasília, mesmo com o voto não sendo obrigatório a partir dos 70 anos. "Eu exerço essa cidadania minha desde que eu comecei a votar. E eu passei um tempo em que a gente não votava, quando eu era mais jovem, por causa da ditadura... Agora, tem que votar todo tempo. Pela democracia", disse ela, que anunciou voto em Lula. "Ele vai ser muito melhor do que essa turma da bala que está aí." Já o também aposentado José Carlos Jarra, de 61 anos, votou em Flávio Bolsonaro em São Paulo. "A gente precisa da mudança. Eu gostaria que ele (Flávio) mudasse a segurança, olhasse mais pelos aposentados, pelo salário mínimo, que aqui no Brasil é uma vergonha. Também rezo para que o Flávio e o Senado mexam neste Supremo Tribunal Federal", afirmou ele. CAMPANHA ENGRENA As três semanas de campanha do segundo turno foram bastante diferentes dos meses que antecederam o primeiro turno, realizado no dia 4 de outubro. No caso de Lula, uma guinada em direção a uma mobilização maciça nas redes sociais e em eventos de rua. Na véspera da votação, antes de participar de evento de campanha em Copacabana, Lula afirmou que "o povo assumiu para si a responsabilidade de fazer a campanha". Um dos destaques da campanha petista no segundo turno foi o impulso nas redes, liderado pelo canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula", criado pelo deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG), que juntou mais de 10 milhões de pessoas para ouvir as "missões" que Janones dava para os apoiadores cumprirem nas redes. A campanha de Flávio chegou a entrar no TSE pedindo a suspensão do canal. A guinada digital da campanha petista teve como ápice Lula -- crítico público do uso frequente de celular que se orgulhava de não ter o aparelho -- ganhando um de presente do governador reeleito do Piauí, Rafael Fonteles (PT), e passando a fazer vários vídeos no formato selfie para apoiadores. Neste quadro, a Meta (META.O) -- proprietária do Facebook, do Instagram e do WhatsApp -- também ficou no foco, após a campanha de Lula apontar que teve sua atuação restrita nas plataformas da empresa, levando a big tech norte-americana a prestar esclarecimentos ao TSE. Do lado de Flávio, após a inesperada liderança no dia 4, o senador deu declarações que geraram polêmica, como quando disse que, se eleito, usará a força que terá no próximo Congresso para alterar a Constituição. Posteriormente, afirmou que iria propor mudanças constitucionais como o fim da reeleição e a redução da maioridade penal. Também acabou mudando de posição em temas pautados por Lula, como o fim da escala de trabalho 6x1, para o qual ele votou favoravelmente no Senado, apesar de, num passado muito recente, ter se declarado contrário. O senador, por outro lado, também conseguiu mobilizar grandes públicos em atos de campanha em todo o país, no que foi uma marca da campanha de ambos os lados. Uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro ampliaria uma onda de triunfos de candidatos de direita na América Latina alinhados ao presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, enquanto um quarto mandato de Lula seria uma decepção para Washington, que teve atritos com o governo do petista em questões de comércio e segurança. Até o momento, Trump evitou declarar apoio a qualquer candidato. Questionado no domingo sobre quem ele gostaria que vencesse, Trump não quis responder. "Não quero entrar nesse assunto, mas estamos acompanhando", disse ele a jornalistas em Washington.

item.title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from Congo
item.description: Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions.
item.dc:creator: Elias Biryabarema
item.content:encoded: Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions. Uganda says it is Ebola-free after [USN:S8N41P031 TEXT:"declaring an end"] to its latest outbreak in July but there has been concern among health experts after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in [USN:SPN45F00J TEXT:"Kenya"] and [USN:L8N4682IW TEXT:"Nigeria"]. Uganda says it investigating the Nigerian case which involves the wife of a Swiss diplomat who visited the country last month. Ugandan officials said they were reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners. Swiss authorities had said the woman contracted the virus in Uganda. Baryomunsi pushed back, saying Switzerland was "speaking prematurely". He said the woman's relatives from West Nile visited her in Kansanga, a suburb of Kampala, and that those relatives had visited Congo. "What evidence do they have that she never travelled there?" he said. "We should speak science, not politics." Kenya's first Ebola patient had travelled from Congo to Uganda and taken a flight from Entebbe airport to Nairobi on Oct. 3. The patient died two days later. Both the Kenyan and the Nigerian cases travelled through the same Ugandan airport on the same day but there was no physical interaction between the two, Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, told the press conference, citing a review of the airport's CCTV system. Baryomunsi said all 60 contacts linked to a [USN:L6N469174 TEXT:"Kenyan Ebola case"] had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged. "The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form," he said. [USN:L1N46915U TEXT:"Genomic analysis"] of Nigeria's only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya's index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection. Uganda borders Congo, where the outbreak began, and has previously battled Ebola outbreaks.

item.title: Trump campaigns in Michigan a day after Obama rallies Democrats
item.description: US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections. Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests, an open-seat race between former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that will help decide control of the chamber. Despite repeatedly attacking El-Sayed from the Oval Office and at rallies across the country, the Republican president had not yet campaigned in Michigan this year. If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist and repeatedly [USN:L1N4620ZA TEXT:"mocked his middle name,"] Mohamed, a common Muslim name. EL-SAYED SAYS AFFILIATION IS WITH THE US El-Sayed has dismissed the accusation and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there’s just too little of in Washington." Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has [USN:L6N4661FE TEXT:"ties to the Muslim Brotherhood"], one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups. In an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Rogers said El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about those allegations. "He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said. El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group, saying it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States. At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks on El-Sayed as an attempt by opponents to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are." The former president compared it to his experience as the target of [USN:KBN23O2P2 TEXT:"false claims"] that he was born in Kenya. "We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." MANUFACTURING INVESTMENTS Trump's rally in Port Huron, part of an area of Michigan that he won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote, will also highlight the US-Canada tariff standoff. The trade fight has affected the Detroit-based [USN:L6N44N11O TEXT:"US auto industry,"] prompting Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy. Rogers on Sunday hailed Trump's tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said "the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit." "There's some good and there's some things we have to work on," he told "Meet the Press." In a Fox News interview ahead of Sunday's rally, Trump praised Rogers as someone who shares Michigan voters' beliefs. "He's going to be an amazing senator," Trump told the "Sunday Briefing" program. "Solid as a rock. Apple pie." Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

item.title: Russia says it hit two cargo vessels and Ukrainian logistics hubs
item.description: The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Russian Defence Ministry said on Sunday that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian forces also hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. The ministry said the facilities had been used for storage and distribution of dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian military. Reuters could not independently verify the Defence Ministry's information.

item.title: Four killed in two drone attacks in Russia's Belgorod region
item.description: A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person and wounded one other in a nearby village.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person and wounded one other in a nearby village. "Unfortunately, the death toll from last night's attack (in the city of Belgorod) has risen — another man who had been injured has died in hospital. This is a great tragedy for all the city's residents," Belgorod's mayor, Valentin Demidov, wrote on state-backed messaging app MAX. The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities, regional governor Alexander Shuvayev said. In a separate incident on Sunday morning, one person was killed and another injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a car in the village of Voznesenovka near the town of Shebekino, local authorities said.

item.title: Brazil votes in tense runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro
item.description: Corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling dominated the race.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Lisandra Paraguassu
item.content:encoded: Brazilians voted on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could move Latin America's largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region. The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored [USN:L6N45Q04L TEXT:"a major upset at the start of the month"] by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round. Tensions were high as polls predicted an incredibly close race, and both candidates made last-minute pleas to electoral authorities to extend voting by two hours in select states. Bolsonaro asked for extra time in three states, citing bad weather, while Lula asked electoral authorities to extend voting in nine states after his campaign alleged officials reduced election day public transportation. Many Brazilians rely on public transport to vote in the cities they are registered in but may not currently reside. Lula's supporters tend to rely more heavily on public transportation in these cities. A court in Bahia state, a Lula stronghold in the Northeast, ordered the arrest of a top transportation official in Salvador over allegations that he directed a reduction in the city’s bus fleet. “Nobody should give up voting because some unscrupulous businessman or some corrupt, dishonest mayor tried to prevent them from doing so," Lula told journalists. WASHINGTON DENIES ACCUSATIONS OF MEDDLING A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. Lula and his allies see Sunday’s runoff as a chance to stem the region's conservative drift. Reuters on Saturday [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"revealed a campaign"] within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power. Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say. "I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington. Brazil's election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from [USN:L1N43T0Q4 TEXT:"Jair Bolsonaro's 2025"] conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if elected. Trump has called the case a "witch hunt" and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While this was later watered down, Trump unleashed [USN:L1N43P1HE TEXT:"new levies against Brazil this year"], citing unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying. “We can’t just hand Brazil over,” said Elenildes dos Reis, a 60-year-old lawyer in Sao Paulo who voted for Lula and said his victory would be a way of standing up to Trump and what she described as a rising wave of fascism. On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds. Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses. “We need change,” said Jose Carlos Jarra, a 61-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo who worked in healthcare and voted for Bolsonaro. He hoped the senator would tackle public security and do more for retirees. In Rio de Janeiro, 75-year-old retiree Alba Marques said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party, not for Bolsonaro. "I can’t stand 40 years of a guy saying he’s going to fix Brazil anymore. The same promise," she said. CANDIDATES ARE NECK AND NECK Casting his ballot in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, Bolsonaro urged people to come out to vote "come rain or shine." Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, near Sao Paulo, and thanked his supporters. "What the people did for me these past few days is something I can never repay," he told reporters. Polls show the candidates practically tied going into the runoff. Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote. Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%. The senator's first-round win [USN:L6N45Q08A TEXT:"sent Brazil's markets and currency soaring"] on expectations of pro-business reforms. His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula.

item.title: Borr Drilling rig sinks off Gabon, one person dead and four missing
item.description: Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one employee and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, three sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Gnaneshwar Rajan, Colleen Goko
item.content:encoded: Borr Drilling's (BORR.N) Prospector 5 rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one employee and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, three sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday. An Indian national, one of the five initially unaccounted for, has been found dead. The remaining four missing include three Gabonese nationals and one other expatriate, the sources said. The government has not confirmed the death, instead saying that five people remain missing and that search efforts were ongoing. "Preliminary information indicates that the rig experienced a punch-through event during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig," the offshore drilling contractor said. The Prospector 5 oil and gas rig, owned and operated by Borr, is contracted to support BW Energy's (BWE.OL) drilling operations off Gabon. The rig had not yet begun drilling. Prospector 5 is located at the Dussafu Marin permit, a licence off the Gabon coast. BW Energy holds a 73.5% working interest in the licence, with Panoro Energy holding 17.5%. Gabon's Ministry of Petroleum and Gas said it had activated a crisis unit and ordered the navy to reinforce search and rescue operations at sea. The ministry also ordered a technical investigation, Petroleum and Gas Minister Clotaire Kondja said in a statement. The crisis unit brings together the ministry, the navy, state oil company Gabon Oil, BW Energy and Borr Drilling, Kondja said. The accident occurred at approximately 9:40 p.m. (2040 GMT) on Saturday in the Dussafu Marin permit area near the Mabomont production facility, the ministry said. "We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident," said Borr Drilling Chief Executive Bruno Morand. "Our immediate priority is supporting the ongoing search and rescue efforts and the welfare of all personnel involved." Panoro Energy (PENR.OL) said production had been halted, adding that there were no reports of damage or accidental discharges. No discharge of harmful substances has been observed, the ministry said, adding that pollution-response resources remained deployed to protect the coastline and nearby Mayumba National Park.

item.title: Elections législatives en Serbie, l'opposition espère renverser Vucic
item.description: Les Serbes se sont massivement rendu aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les Serbes se sont massivement rendu aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption. Aleksandar Vucic a démissionné de ses fonctions de président le mois dernier après avoir annoncé la tenue d'élections anticipées, dans une tentative visant à prolonger son emprise sur le pouvoir en se présentant à nouveau au poste de Premier ministre. De longues files se sont formées devant les bureaux de vote dans tout le pays, et même Aleksandar Vucic a dû patienter deux heures avant de déposer son bulletin dans l'urne. A 18h00, le taux de participation s'élevait à 67,6%, le plus élevé depuis l'éclatement de la Yougoslavie en 1992. Les bureaux de vote ont fermé à 20h00 (19h00 GMT). Les premiers résultats sont attendus environ deux heures plus tard. Aleksandar Vucic a été confronté à des manifestations anti-corruption déclenchées par l'effondrement, en novembre 2024, du toit de la gare de la ville de Novi Sad, dans le nord du pays, qui a tué 16 personnes. Une victoire de l'opposition estudiantine constituerait un profond bouleversement politique dans ce pays des Balkans comptant quelque 6 millions d'habitants. Elle pourrait également servir de modèle à d'autres mouvements étudiants à travers l'Europe, qui sont descendus dans la rue ces dernières semaines pour protester, parfois violemment, contre la mauvaise qualité de l'enseignement et le manque de perspectives d'avenir. Depuis son accession au pouvoir en 2014, Aleksandar Vucic a supervisé une période de développement économique mais a également dû faire face à un mécontentement croissant face à ce que ses opposants qualifient de corruption et d'autoritarisme. Il bénéficie toutefois du soutien de sa formation, le Parti progressiste serbe, qui l'a désigné comme candidat au poste de Premier ministre.

item.title: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midterms
item.description: Barack Obama framed the Nov. 3 midterm elections vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency.
item.dc:creator: Dan Catchpole
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that. Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations. Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration. Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency. "We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," Obama said. Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative. The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats' frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans' willingness to go along with him. "We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this," Obama said. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this ... Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But in a Truth Social post on early Sunday morning, Trump called Obama a "grossly incompetent President" and labeled El-Sayed a "Muslim Brotherhood Jihadist, who hates Jews and Blacks and AMERICANS and TRUMP". A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have [USN:L6N44F13X TEXT:"inappropriately profited"] from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings. Obama also ridiculed the administration's claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters. "Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world," Obama said. In his social media post, Trump derided the Obama administration's approach to the Iranians, saying that he "paid off Iran with $Billions, and gave them a road to a Nuclear Weapon" with his 2015 [USN:L6N42K0ZD TEXT:"Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action"] accord with Iran. The United States withdrew from the 2015 agreement during Trump's first term. The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasizing unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth someone "laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops" and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said.

item.title: Serbia votes in historic election as students seek to end Vucic's long grip on power
item.description: Serbians voted in record numbers in Sunday's parliamentary election as a mass student protest movement sought to unseat longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
item.dc:creator: Ivana Sekularac, Edward Mcallister, Aleksandar Vasovic
item.content:encoded: Serbians voted in record numbers in Sunday's parliamentary election as a mass student protest movement sought to unseat longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade. The [USN:L8N46618N TEXT:"snap parliamentary elections"], called by Vucic in September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since [USN:L8N4650K6 TEXT:"gained widespread support"]. Long lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote. Pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put turnout at 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. Polls closed at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) and first indications of results are expected around 10 p.m. A student victory would be a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the [USN:L1N40V01B TEXT:"defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban"] in April. It could also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"taken to the streets"] in recent weeks to protest, [USN:L2N46A01A TEXT:"in some cases violently"], against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. "(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. OPINION POLLS PREDICTED TIGHT RACE Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Internationally, he has sought closer ties with China, a major investor, and remained close to Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas. At the same time, he still says he wants to join the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner, but the bloc has become [USN:L6N3Z90I6 TEXT:"increasingly frustrated"] with a lack of reform. "I voted for our children, our young people...our children deserve peace and work, only Vucic can bring that," said Hatidza, a Roma woman. The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is not clear who would be prime minister should they win. "I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," Srdanovic said after casting his vote in Novi Sad early in the morning. After casting his vote, Vucic said he would respect the result. "If we lose we will acknowledge the will of the electorate, if we win no one will take it (from us)," he said. Opinion polls ahead of the vote had predicted a tight race to win the 250-seat parliament. The head of the Election Commission, Vladimir Dimitrijevic, said voting had passed without incident, but the EU's ambassador to Serbia, Andreas von Beckerath, expressed concern in a post on X about "reported violent incidents" at several polling stations. Monitoring bodies CeSID and CRTA pointed to incidents related to the electoral roll and secrecy of voting. STUDENT PROTESTS INCREASE PRESSURE ON VUCIC The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say [USN:L8N4612LD TEXT:"repression has worsened"] in the period since. "For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. "This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia."

item.title: Sydney's new international airport opens to passengers
item.description: Sydney's new A$5.6 billion ($3.94 billion) airport opened to passengers on Sunday after more than a decade of planning, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was a milestone for the country's most populous city.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Sydney's new A$5.6 billion ($3.94 billion) airport opened to passengers on Sunday after more than a decade of planning, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was a milestone for the country's most populous city. The new Western Sydney International Airport in Badgerys Creek, about 60 km (37.3 miles) west of central Sydney, will operate 24 hours a day, giving [USN:L1N42I00H TEXT:"airlines"] access to a fast-growing and ethnically diverse population centre. The current airport, located closer to Sydney's central business district, can host takeoffs and landings only until 11 p.m. and after 6 a.m., limiting airline scheduling options relative to other major Australian cities like Melbourne. "For the first time in more than 50 years, Australia is opening a major new airport. It’s a milestone that has been decades in the making," Albanese said in a statement. "I’m very proud to officially open it," he said. Qantas' (QAN.AX) budget arm Jetstar was due to operate the first outbound flight to the Gold Coast on Sunday, the airport said in a statement. The airport has capacity for more than 80 million passenger movements annually, it said. The start of passenger services comes after cargo flights commenced at the facility in July. Located on a 1,780-hectare (4,398-acre) site purchased by the federal government in the 1980s, the airport was completed in July 2025 after a seven-year build and 15 years of planning. ($1 = 1.4219 Australian dollars)

item.title: Saudis say Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
item.description: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target". King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the militant group continued unabated. The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked. The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran , turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. FLIGHT TRACKING DATA SHOWS LITTLE TRAFFIC After Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would "never be safe" and urged airlines, airport staff and travellers not to use it. Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday. Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11. MISSILE AND DRONE ATTACKS CONTINUE Saudi civil defense said on Sunday that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles. Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed. The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements. Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier.

item.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
item.description: Two US State Department officials pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who [USN:L1N3ZM12Y TEXT:"oversees Brazil policy"], and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"27-year sentence in September 2025"], the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of " free speech diplomacy ," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those [USN:S0N3ON011 TEXT:"announced against Mexican cartels"] in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O) - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March [USN:S0N3ZG01R TEXT:"Brazil barred Beattie"] from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

item.title: Audi defends decision to stand by Trump on $4 billion US factory in Georgia
item.description: Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a $1.4 billion blow last year.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, David Shepardson, Rachel More
item.content:encoded: The head of German automaker Audi defended on Sunday the company's planned $4 billion investment in a new US plant, announced by President Donald Trump as he campaigns for the November midterm elections . Audi Chief Executive Gernot Doellner stood alongside Trump at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia on Saturday, as the US president said Audi, part of the Volkswagen Group , planned to build an assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually. "This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations," Doellner told reporters on Sunday. "If the American president invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands." A final decision on the investment will have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board for it to go ahead. Georgia has competitive election races for the US Senate and its governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy and boosting US manufacture. In Germany, the tariffs have added to the pressures on European industry and [USN:L8N4690LO TEXT:"tension between"] Volkswagen management and workers, who face job cuts and possible plant closures. Trump's tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts cost Audi around €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) last year as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico, Audi has said. Critics of the tariffs say they have also been damaging in the US where they have increased vehicle prices and delayed some automaker investments. A spokesperson for Germany's IG Metall union said the decision by Doellner to extend a hand to Trump during the election was "hard to understand". "Trump has never failed to make it clear what he is after: he wants to weaken our domestic economy, particularly the automotive sector," the spokesperson said. Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair, said it was "right and necessary" to improve the company's position on the US market with a new plant. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out," she said. Doellner declined to give full details on the investment deal with the US, including whether it involves tariff relief for the company. AN OPPORTUNITY IF GERMAN WORKERS BENEFIT Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." A gold Audi with manufacturer licence plates was parked outside Trump's rally on Saturday.

item.description: La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela CARACAS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - La cheffe de file de l'opposition vénézuélienne, Maria Corina Machado, a annoncé dimanche être rentrée dans son pays après avoir passé près d'un an dans la clandestinité à l'étranger. Elections législatives en Serbie, l'opposition tente de renverser Vucic BELGRADE, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Serbes se rendent aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption. Les Brésiliens aux urnes pour un second tour serré entre Lula et Bolsonaro SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Brésiliens ont commencé à voter dimanche pour un second tour de la présidentielle qui s'annonce serré et qui pourrait faire basculer le plus grand pays d'Amérique latine vers la droite, comme nombre de pays de la région. Ouchakov, conseiller de Poutine, prône une implication européenne dans les efforts de paix en Ukraine MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Europe doit être impliquée dans les discussions sur une issue au conflit entre l'Ukraine et la Russie car sa position pourrait être déterminante, a déclaré dimanche Iouri Ouchakov, conseiller diplomatique du président russe Vladimir Poutine. L'Arabie saoudite intercepte des missiles et des drones 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Arabie saoudite a intercepté dimanche des drones et des missiles au-dessus de sa capitale Ryad et du sud de son territoire, a dit la coalition emmenée par les Saoudiens contre les Houthis au Yémen. Russie-Trois morts dans des attaques dans la région de Belgorod MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont été tuées et 13 autres blessées dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche par une attaque de drone ukrainienne contre la ville de Belgorod, en Russie, près de la frontière entre les deux pays, ont déclaré les autorités locales. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Brésil-Lula et Bolsonaro mobilisent leurs partisans à la veille du second tour de la présidentielle SÃO PAULO, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Le président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva et le sénateur Flavio Bolsonaro ont clôturé samedi leur campagne en vue du second tour de l'élection présidentielle au Brésil, en mobilisant leurs partisans et en lançant un dernier appel aux électeurs indécis. Election présidentielle en Bulgarie dans un contexte d'attaques en mer Noire SOFIA, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bulgares sont appelés aux urnes dimanche pour une élection présidentielle qui intervient alors que la guerre en Ukraine s'étend au large de la côte bulgare en mer Noire. Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens.
